title: NYC regulates residential density by floor area ratio
statement: Maximum zoning floor area equals the district FAR multiplied by the zoning-lot area. Zoning floor area is a defined measurement that excludes cellars, mechanical space and exempt amenity, corridor and refuse space, so it differs from physical gross building area and from net rentable or sellable area. There is no apartments-per-acre limit; in R6 to R12 the 680 square foot dwelling-unit factor caps unit count outside special density areas.
qualifiers: Special purpose districts can modify FAR and the unit factor.
Model zoning floor area, gross area and net saleable area separately.
misconceptions: Treating FAR times lot area as gross building area or as rentable area.
questions: How is buildable floor area calculated in NYC?
Does NYC limit units per acre?
What is the difference between zoning floor area and gross area?

title: Who can use the qualifying (higher) residential FAR and height
statement: The higher column in the R6 to R12 FAR and height tables applies only to qualifying affordable housing or qualifying senior housing. Qualifying affordable housing means an MIH development in an MIH area, a UAP development, or a building under an affordable housing regulatory agreement. Qualifying senior housing means affordable independent residences for seniors or long-term care facilities. Under UAP the FAR may exceed the standard figure only by the amount of affordable floor area provided.
qualifiers: A project with some lower-rent units does not qualify unless it meets one of these definitions.
misconceptions: Assuming the qualifying FAR is unrestricted market-rate capacity.
questions: What is qualifying affordable housing?
Who gets the higher FAR in the residential table?
Does senior housing get extra FAR?

title: R4 and R5 basic residential FAR
statement: R4, R4A, R4B and R4-1 allow 1.00 FAR, or 1.50 on qualifying residential sites. R5, R5A and R5B allow 1.50, or 2.00 on qualifying residential sites. R5D allows 2.00 in both cases. Predominantly built-up area rules allow 1.35 in R4 and 1.65 in R5.
qualifiers: Subdistrict, lower-density growth management area and special-district rules can change these figures.
questions: What FAR is allowed in R4?
What FAR is allowed in R5?

title: R6B FAR and height
statement: R6B: standard residential FAR 2.00 and maximum height 55 ft; qualifying affordable or senior housing FAR 2.40 and maximum height 65 ft. Base height 30 to 45 ft.
qualifiers: Before special-district rules and §23-443 height modifications.
questions: What is the FAR in R6B?
How tall can a building be in R6B?

title: R6A FAR and height
statement: R6A: standard residential FAR 3.00 and maximum height 75 ft; qualifying affordable or senior housing FAR 3.90 and maximum height 95 ft. The same values apply to R6 within 100 ft of a wide street and to R6-1.
qualifiers: Before special-district rules and §23-443 height modifications.
questions: What is the FAR in R6A?
How tall can a building be in R6A?

title: R7A FAR and height
statement: R7A: standard residential FAR 4.00 and maximum height 85 ft; qualifying affordable or senior housing FAR 5.01 and maximum height 115 ft. The UAP increase from 4.00 to 5.01 is 25.25 percent. R7-1 and R7-2 within 100 ft of a wide street use the same FAR; beyond 100 ft their standard FAR is 3.44, so the UAP increase there is 45.6 percent.
qualifiers: Before special-district rules and §23-443 height modifications.
Outside MIH areas the increase is usable only as affordable floor area.
questions: What is the FAR in R7A?
How much does UAP add in R7A?

title: R7D FAR and height
statement: R7D: standard residential FAR 4.66 and maximum height 105 ft; qualifying affordable or senior housing FAR 5.60 and maximum height 125 ft.
qualifiers: Before special-district rules and §23-443 height modifications.
questions: What is the FAR in R7D?

title: R7X FAR and height
statement: R7X: standard residential FAR 5.00 and maximum height 125 ft; qualifying affordable or senior housing FAR 6.00 and maximum height 145 ft.
qualifiers: Before special-district rules and §23-443 height modifications.
questions: What is the FAR in R7X?

title: R8A FAR and height
statement: R8A: standard residential FAR 6.02 and maximum height 125 ft; qualifying affordable or senior housing FAR 7.20 and maximum height 145 ft. On a 20,000 square foot lot that is 120,400 standard versus 144,000 qualifying zoning square feet, an increase of 23,600.
qualifiers: No wide or narrow street split.
Outside MIH areas the 23,600 square foot increment is usable only as affordable floor area.
questions: What is the FAR in R8A?
How tall can a building be in R8A?

title: R8X FAR and height
statement: R8X: standard residential FAR 6.02 and maximum height 155 ft; qualifying affordable or senior housing FAR 7.20 and maximum height 175 ft.
qualifiers: Before special-district rules and §23-443 height modifications.
questions: What is the FAR in R8X?

title: R9A FAR and height
statement: R9A: standard residential FAR 7.52; qualifying affordable or senior housing FAR 9.02. Standard maximum height is 145 ft within 100 ft of a wide street and 135 ft elsewhere; qualifying maximum height is 185 ft in both locations. Maximum base height is 105 ft on a wide street and 95 ft on a narrow street.
qualifiers: The wide-street portion follows the lot-portion tests in §23-432 footnotes.
R9A cannot use tower rules.
questions: What is the FAR in R9A?
How tall can a building be in R9A?

title: R10A FAR and height
statement: R10A: standard residential FAR 10.00; qualifying affordable or senior housing FAR 12.00. Standard maximum height is 215 ft within 100 ft of a wide street and 185 ft elsewhere; qualifying maximum height is 235 ft. Minimum base height is 125 ft within 100 ft of a wide street and 60 ft elsewhere; maximum base height on a wide street is 155 ft.
qualifiers: R10A cannot use tower rules or eligible-site heights, so these caps hold.
R10 without a suffix can use towers or a 355 ft eligible-site height.
questions: What is the FAR in R10A?
How tall can a building be in R10A?

title: R11 and R11A FAR and height
statement: R11 and R11A: standard residential FAR 12.00 and maximum height 255 ft; qualifying affordable or senior housing FAR 15.00 and maximum height 325 ft. R11 without a suffix can exceed the table height through tower rules or a 405 ft eligible-site height. R11A has the same heights as R11 but can use neither alternative; its minimum base height is 125 ft within 100 ft of a wide street.
qualifiers: R11 is mapped only through rezonings that carry MIH, so UAP is not available there in practice.
misconceptions: Saying R11A is the alternative that changes R11 heights; the alternatives are towers and eligible-site heights.
questions: What is the FAR in R11?
How tall can a building be in R11?

title: R12 FAR and height
statement: R12: standard residential FAR 15.00 and maximum height 325 ft; qualifying affordable or senior housing FAR 18.00 and maximum height 395 ft. R12 can exceed the table height through tower rules or a 495 ft eligible-site height.
qualifiers: R12 is mapped only through rezonings that carry MIH, so UAP is not available there in practice.
questions: What is the FAR in R12?
How tall can a building be in R12?

title: Citywide height modifications that apply before special-district rules
statement: The R6 to R12 height tables are modified citywide by §23-443: transition areas next to R1 to R5 district boundaries cap heights at 45 to 85 ft; frontage next to transportation infrastructure adds 20 ft in R7 to R12; Limited Height Districts cap standard heights; and an adjoining public park counts as a wide street when §23-381 is used. Eligible-site heights under §23-434 apply only to districts without a letter suffix.
qualifiers: Special purpose districts can modify heights further.
misconceptions: Reading the §23-432 table as the final height without checking §23-443.
questions: What can change the maximum height in a residential district?
Do transition areas limit height?

title: Wide street and narrow street
statement: A wide street is any street 75 ft or more in width; a narrow street is less than 75 ft. Named segments also count as wide streets, including Broadway between W 94th and W 97th Streets and the Allen Street roadways between Rivington and Delancey Streets (added March 26, 2026). In C5-3, C6-4 and C6-6 districts certain 65 to 70 ft segments can count.
qualifiers: Wide-street status changes setbacks, base heights and, in R9A and R10A, maximum height.
questions: What counts as a wide street?
Is Allen Street a wide street?

title: Base heights and upper setbacks in R6 to R12
statement: Each district sets a minimum and maximum base (street-wall) height, for example R6B 30 to 45 ft and R10A 125 to 155 ft on a wide street. Above the base, the standard setback is at least 10 ft on a wide street and at least 15 ft on a narrow street. The setback is reduced 1 ft for each foot the street wall is recessed, to a minimum of 7 ft, and is optional for portions beyond 50 ft of the street line.
qualifiers: Dormers and other exceptions apply under §23-433.
questions: What is the required setback above the base height?
What base height is allowed?

title: Residential rear yard depth
statement: For detached and zero lot line buildings, and for semi-detached or attached buildings on zoning lots 40 ft or wider, the rear yard is at least 20 ft for portions at or below 75 ft, and 30 ft for portions above 75 ft. Semi-detached and attached buildings on lots narrower than 40 ft need at least 30 ft. Shallow interior lots under 95 ft deep that existed on December 15, 1961 may reduce the depth by 6 inches per foot of shortfall, to a minimum of 10 ft. Corner lots need no rear yard; through lots use rear yard equivalents.
qualifiers: Applies in all residence districts on interior lots.
misconceptions: Saying the rear yard is commonly 30 ft; that was the rule before December 5, 2024. The 2025 Zoning Handbook calls 20 ft typical.
questions: How deep must a rear yard be?
Is the rear yard 20 or 30 feet?

title: Lot coverage and lot types in R6 to R12
statement: Maximum residential lot coverage in R6 to R12 is 80 percent on interior and through lots and 100 percent on corner lots. §23-363 raises coverage for shallow lots, portions within 100 ft of a corner and along the short end of a block. Interior, corner and through lots carry different yard rules, and coverage can prevent a building from reaching its full FAR.
questions: What lot coverage is allowed?
Do corner lots have different rules?

title: Residential tower rules
statement: Towers are permitted in R9 to R12 other than R9A, R9X, R10A and R11A. Tower coverage is limited to 65 percent of the lot up to 300 ft and 50 percent above. In R9 and R10, §23-441 adds tower-on-a-base rules near wide streets and bars towers within 100 ft of a public park of one acre or more.
misconceptions: Assuming an R10 site is limited to roughly 20 stories; an R10 without a suffix can use towers.
questions: Where are towers allowed?
Can R10A use tower rules?

title: Amenity, corridor and refuse floor area exclusions
statement: In buildings with multiple dwellings, resident-accessible amenity space is excluded from floor area up to 5 percent of the residential floor area; corridors and vertical circulation do not count as amenity space. Separately, 50 percent of qualifying corridor space is excluded under §23-232, and refuse space up to 3 square feet per dwelling unit under §23-233. A building with 100,000 square feet of residential floor area can exclude up to 5,000 square feet of amenities.
questions: Is amenity space counted as floor area?
Are corridors excluded from FAR?

title: Dwelling unit factor (maximum number of units)
statement: For multiple dwellings, the maximum number of units is the maximum residential floor area permitted on the zoning lot divided by 680; a fraction of three-quarters or more counts as one unit. No factor applies to developments and enlargements in special density areas (the Manhattan Core and the Special Downtown Brooklyn District), to qualifying senior housing, to conversions of non-residential buildings in special density areas, or to conversions of community facility buildings anywhere. A 10,000 square foot R7A lot at 4.00 FAR has a 59-unit cap (40,000 / 680 = 58.82); at the qualifying 5.01 FAR the cap is 73 units (50,100 / 680 = 73.68).
qualifiers: Does not apply to one- and two-family residences.
Building code, light and air, accessibility and legal layouts can reduce the count further.
misconceptions: Dividing net area by an average unit size (for example 64 units) without checking the 680 cap.
questions: How many apartments can I build?
What is the dwelling unit factor?
Is there a unit limit in Manhattan?

title: Manhattan Core
statement: The Manhattan Core is Manhattan Community Districts 1 through 8. It reaches E 96th Street on the East Side and W 110th Street on the West Side, and includes Roosevelt Island. It matters for MIH (the Workforce option is unavailable there) and for unit counts (it is a special density area with no dwelling unit factor).
misconceptions: Describing the Manhattan Core as Manhattan south of 96th Street; that HPD shorthand omits the Upper West Side between 96th and 110th Streets and Roosevelt Island.
questions: What is the Manhattan Core?
Is the Upper West Side in the Manhattan Core?

title: R1 to R3 residence districts
statement: R1 and R2 are single-family detached districts. R3A, R3X and R3-1 allow single- or two-family residences. R3-2 is a general residence district that allows all housing types.
qualifiers: City of Yes for Housing Opportunity added accessory dwelling units and qualifying residential sites in low-density districts.
questions: What can be built in R1, R2 or R3?

title: Housing in commercial districts and residential equivalents
statement: C1 and C2 are local commercial districts. The overlays C1-1 to C1-5 and C2-1 to C2-5 take their bulk from the surrounding residence district; C1-6 to C1-9 and C2-6 to C2-8 are mapped districts with a residential equivalent. Residences are permitted in every C4 district (C4-1 equals R5 up to C4-12 equals R12), C5 (R10 and higher) and C6 (R6 to R12). The equivalence table is §34-112 and §35-23 applies the equivalent's residential bulk. C7 and C8 exclude new residences and have no residential equivalent.
qualifiers: Special districts can change these rules.
misconceptions: Assuming a commercial designation such as C6 prohibits apartments.
questions: Can I build apartments in a commercial district?
What is the residential equivalent of C6-2?
Is housing allowed in C8?

title: Housing in manufacturing districts
statement: Manufacturing districts exclude new residences, with M1 exceptions: artists' joint living-work quarters in M1-5B; dwelling units in M1-5M, M1-6M and M1-6D; dwelling units in M1-1D to M1-5D by City Planning Commission authorization; and M1 districts paired with a residence district in Special Mixed Use (MX) Districts, where both districts' uses are permitted. M2 and M3 allow no new residences, and M3 also excludes community facilities.
qualifiers: In MX districts the paired residence district cannot be R1 or R2.
misconceptions: Saying M1 never allows housing.
questions: Can I build housing in an M1 district?
What is an MX district?

title: Zoning lot mergers and air rights
statement: Tax lots can form one zoning lot, letting unused floor area move within it, without a rezoning. The lots must be on the same block and contiguous for at least 10 linear feet. A declaration of restrictions must be executed by all parties in interest, including holders of superior recorded interests such as mortgagees, or waived by them, supported by a title certificate and recorded. Rights do not move between unrelated sites elsewhere in the city.
qualifiers: Check existing declarations, prior transfers and envelope fit before paying for rights.
questions: How do I buy air rights from a neighbor?
What is a zoning lot merger?

title: Landmark development rights transfer by certification
statement: Under §75-422 a transfer from a landmark may not raise the receiving lot's maximum floor area by more than 20 percent, or 30 percent in commercial or manufacturing districts whose maximum non-residential FAR is 15.0 or more. Receiving lots must be in the surrounding area (same block, across a street or intersection, or a chain of lots in 15+ FAR commercial districts) and in common ownership (§75-421). Certification requires a joint application, site plans and calculations, a continuing maintenance program for the landmark with a Landmarks Preservation Commission report, and recorded transfer instruments and notices of restriction.
qualifiers: There is no §75-423 in the current text.
questions: How much landmark air rights can a site receive?
What is the landmark transfer cap?

title: Landmark transfers above the certification cap
statement: A landmark transfer above 30 percent is possible only by a §74-79 special permit (subject to ULURP), and only in commercial or manufacturing districts with a maximum non-residential FAR of 15.0 or more. Everywhere else the 20 percent cap is absolute, except for special-district programs such as East Midtown and the Theater Subdistrict. In those other districts §74-79 allows bulk modifications only, and §75-24 authorizations allow non-FAR bulk changes with height increases of no more than 25 percent.
misconceptions: Saying transfers above the cap simply use separate rules anywhere.
questions: Can a landmark transfer exceed 20 percent?
What does 74-79 allow?

title: Mass transit station improvement bonus
statement: A general bonus of up to 20 percent of floor area is available for major station improvements on qualifying transit improvement sites: R9 to R12 districts and their commercial equivalents, C7-6 to C7-9, M1 paired with R9 to R12, and M1-6, M1-7A, M1-8A and M1-9A, within 500 ft of a station (1,500 ft in central business districts). It is granted by City Planning Commission authorization (up to 200,000 square feet) or special permit. Special districts have their own transit bonuses.
qualifiers: Combined bonuses are capped at 20 percent unless a special district or special permit provides otherwise (§66-513).
Discretionary; proximity to a subway alone does not qualify a site.
misconceptions: Saying transit bonuses exist only in special districts.
questions: Is there a bonus for subway improvements?
Can I get extra FAR near a subway station?

title: Public plaza bonus
statement: The §33-13 public plaza bonus is available in listed high-density commercial districts (C1-8, C1-9, C2-7, C2-8, C4-6 to C4-12, C5-1 to C5-5, C6-1 to C6-12, C7-5 to C7-9) and adds commercial or community facility floor area only. §24-14 offers a plaza bonus of 6 square feet per square foot of plaza in R9 to R12 for buildings that are 25 percent or less residential. There is no residential plaza bonus in Article II Chapter 3, and the bonus is not citywide.
qualifiers: Plaza design, public access and approval standards apply.
misconceptions: Counting a plaza bonus toward residential floor area.
questions: Does a public plaza earn bonus floor area?
Can a plaza bonus add apartments?

title: Do not add bonuses and transfers together without checking caps
statement: UAP, zoning lot mergers, landmark transfers, transit bonuses, rezonings and floor area exclusions each have their own eligibility, compatibility and cap rules. §66-513 caps combined bonuses at 20 percent unless a special district or special permit says otherwise, and §75-422 caps landmark transfers. Check the combination caps for the specific site rather than summing percentages, and keep zoning floor area, gross area and saleable area in separate models.
qualifiers: Some combinations are legal; the rule is to verify them, not to assume they are barred.
misconceptions: Summing bonus percentages to estimate total capacity.
questions: Can I combine UAP with air rights?
Can bonuses be stacked?

title: Universal Affordability Preference (UAP) eligibility and process
statement: UAP applies to developments and enlargements outside Mandatory Inclusionary Housing areas in R6 and higher districts and their residential equivalents. It lets residential FAR exceed the standard figure, up to the qualifying FAR, only by the amount of permanently affordable floor area provided. It is as-of-right (no City Planning Commission or BSA approval), but HPD must approve the affordable housing application, a restrictive declaration must be recorded, HPD issues a permit notice before DOB permits, and a completion notice before the permanent certificate of occupancy.
qualifiers: HPD describes UAP as R6 to R10 because R11 and R12 are mapped only through rezonings that carry MIH.
Standalone conversions are not UAP developments, although affordable floor area may be supplied through a conversion (§27-14).
Special purpose districts can modify the rules.
HPD approval timing is on the critical path.
misconceptions: Treating UAP floor area as unrestricted market-rate capacity.
Assuming as-of-right means no agency approval.
questions: What is UAP?
Does UAP apply in an MIH area?
Is UAP as of right?

title: UAP affordability requirements
statement: UAP affordable units are restricted for the regulatory period, which lasts as long as the affordable floor area supports the development (HPD calls them permanently income-restricted). Households must average no more than 60 percent of the income index at initial occupancy, using no more than three income bands, in multiples of 10 percent, none above 100 percent. Where a site has 10,000 square feet or more of affordable floor area, at least 20 percent of that affordable floor area must be at a band of 40 percent or less.
qualifiers: Affordable floor area includes a prorated share of eligible common areas, which affects the 10,000 square foot test.
UAP has no off-site option except in UAP Offsite Option Areas (former Inclusionary Housing designated areas or R10).
questions: What AMI does UAP require?
How many income bands can UAP use?
Does UAP require deep affordability?

title: Affordable housing regulatory agreement route
statement: Instead of the income-band rules, affordable units may follow an affordable housing regulatory agreement executed after December 5, 2024. The agreement must come with public funding, restrict all units for at least 30 years and, for rentals, restrict the bonus floor area for the life of the building.
qualifiers: Not available to a market-rate project.
misconceptions: Treating the regulatory agreement route as a general alternative for any project.
questions: What is the regulatory agreement alternative under UAP?

title: AMI and the Zoning Resolution income index
statement: The Zoning Resolution measures affordability against the income index: 200 percent of HUD's Very Low-Income Limit for multifamily tax subsidy projects, adjusted for household size by HPD. HPD publishes it as 100 percent AMI in its annual income limits and maximum rents tables. For 2026 HPD changed the studio household factor from 0.7 to 0.6, and until the 2027 AMI is adopted applicants may use either the 2025 AMI (0.7) or the 2026 AMI (0.6).
qualifiers: AMI is an income benchmark, not a share of market rent.
questions: What does AMI mean in NYC zoning?
Which AMI table do I use?

title: Where and how Mandatory Inclusionary Housing applies
statement: In mapped MIH areas (Appendix F or special purpose district text), no residential development, enlargement or conversion from non-residential use is permitted without affordable housing or a fund contribution under one of the options mapped for that area. Requirements are percentages of residential floor area, not unit counts; for an enlargement the base is the enlargement's residential floor area. MIH can also be imposed as a condition of a special permit. The current section is §27-131; older citations such as §23-154 apply only to vested projects.
qualifiers: Reconstructed floor area and units with changed layouts count as part of an enlargement.
misconceptions: Counting MIH percentages by apartments instead of floor area.
questions: Does MIH apply to my site?
Is MIH based on units or floor area?

title: MIH options 1 to 4
statement: Option 1: at least 25 percent of residential floor area at a weighted average of no more than 60 percent AMI, with at least 10 percent of total residential floor area at 40 percent AMI; a 100,000 square foot development provides 25,000 affordable square feet including 10,000 at 40 percent, so the other 15,000 can average up to 73.3 percent. Option 2: 30 percent at 80 percent AMI. Option 3 (Deep Affordability): 20 percent at 40 percent AMI. Options 1 to 3 allow no more than three bands, none above 130 percent. Option 4 (Workforce): 30 percent at 115 percent AMI, up to four bands, none above 135 percent, with at least 5 percent at 70 percent and 5 percent at 90 percent.
qualifiers: Option 3 may not use public funding unless HPD finds it necessary to support a significant amount of additional affordable housing.

Option 4 may not use public funding, can be mapped only together with Option 1, 2 or 3, is unavailable in the Manhattan Core, and expires 10 years after the amendment that establishes or renews it, with vesting under §11-33.
misconceptions: Describing the Workforce option as barred only south of 96th Street; the bar covers Manhattan Community Districts 1 to 8.
questions: What are the MIH options?
What does MIH Option 1 require?
Where is the Workforce option unavailable?

title: MIH small-project exemption and fund option
statement: A single development, enlargement or conversion of no more than 10 dwelling units and no more than 12,500 square feet of residential floor area, on a zoning lot that existed when the MIH area was established, is exempt; both tests must be met. Buildings whose only residences are affordable independent residences for seniors are also exempt, and BSA can grant full waivers under §73-623. Projects that add no more than 25 dwelling units and less than 25,000 square feet of residential floor area may pay into the affordable housing fund instead, at an amount set by HPD's annual schedule; contributions stay in the borough, and in the same community district for at least 10 years.
misconceptions: Using HPD's 'do not exceed 25,000 square feet' wording; the Zoning Resolution says less than 25,000 and controls.
questions: Are small projects exempt from MIH?
Can I pay into a fund instead of building affordable units?

title: MIH off-site compliance
statement: When MIH affordable floor area is provided off-site, the requirement increases by 5 percent of the development's residential floor area multiplied by the share provided off-site. The off-site building must be in the same community district, or in an adjacent community district within half a mile.
qualifiers: Confirm the denominator and common-area allocation before underwriting.
questions: Can MIH units be built off-site?
How much more affordable housing is needed off-site?

title: How UAP, MIH and 485-x relate
statement: UAP is a zoning floor area preference outside MIH areas; MIH is a mandatory set-aside inside mapped MIH areas; 485-x is a separate state property tax exemption administered by HPD. UAP and MIH never apply to the same lot. The same affordable units can likely count toward both a zoning program and 485-x if they meet the stricter terms of each, but this has not been confirmed in an HPD rule.
qualifiers: Underwrite each program's requirements separately and confirm overlap with HPD.
misconceptions: Assuming each program needs its own separate affordable units.
questions: Can affordable units count for both MIH and 485-x?
How do UAP and 485-x interact?

title: 485-x (Affordable Neighborhoods for New Yorkers) basics and deadlines
statement: 485-x is a real property tax exemption for new multiple dwellings and eligible conversions; it grants no zoning floor area. Construction must commence after June 15, 2022 and on or before June 15, 2034 (commencement means excavation and construction of initial footings and foundations lawfully begun in good faith), and be completed on or before June 15, 2038. Projects commencing on or after April 20, 2024 must file a registration notice within six months after commencement; late filing carries a penalty of up to 100 percent of the application fee rather than automatic loss of eligibility.
qualifiers: Its permanent rent stabilization, wage floors and MWBE requirements also reduce NOI.
Construction-period exemption is up to 3 years, or up to 5 years for very large Zone A projects.
misconceptions: Treating 485-x as a source of extra density.
questions: What is 485-x?
What are the 485-x deadlines?
When must a 485-x project register?

title: 485-x rental options A, B and C
statement: Option B (modest rental, 6 to 99 units): at least 20 percent of units affordable at a weighted average of no more than 80 percent AMI; 100 percent exemption for 25 years, then for 10 years only the affordability percentage (for example 20 percent) is exempt. Option A (large rental, 100 or more units): at least 25 percent at no more than 80 percent AMI; 100 percent exemption for 35 years. Option A very large (150 or more units in Zone A or Zone B): at least 25 percent at no more than 60 percent AMI; 100 percent exemption for 40 years. There is no Zone C; a 150+ unit site elsewhere is a large rental project. Option C (small rental, 6 to 10 units outside Manhattan on a zoning lot permitting no more than 12,500 square feet of residential floor area): at least 50 percent of units permanently rent stabilized with no AMI set-aside; 100 percent exemption for 10 years.
qualifiers: Percentages are floors.
Options A and B allow no more than three income bands, none above 100 percent AMI.
The 12,500 square foot test for Option C is what the zoning lot permits, not what is built.
misconceptions: Assuming Option B gets a full exemption for all 35 years.
Assuming the 150-unit category applies outside Zones A and B.
questions: What does 485-x require for a 50-unit building?
How long is the 485-x benefit?
What is 485-x Option C?

title: 485-x Option D homeownership
statement: Option D covers condominium and cooperative projects outside Manhattan with an average assessed value at or below $89 per square foot at first assessment, and a 5-year primary residence agreement. The benefit is 100 percent for 14 years and 25 percent for 6 years, with no exemption on assessed value above $89 per square foot.
qualifiers: Option D has no affordable-unit set-aside; its restriction period is 20 years.
questions: Does 485-x cover condos?
What is 485-x Option D?

title: 485-x affordable unit mix, distribution and permanence
statement: 485-x set-asides count dwelling units, not floor area. Affordable units must either match the market-rate unit mix proportionally, or be at least 50 percent two-bedroom or larger with no more than 25 percent smaller than one bedroom. HPD rules require affordable units in every building segment in similar proportion and limit clustering on a floor. For rental projects the restriction runs in perpetuity, and restricted units remain rent stabilized.
misconceptions: Assuming small affordable units can satisfy the count.
questions: Do 485-x affordable units need to match the bedroom mix?
Are 485-x units permanent?

title: 485-x Zone A and Zone B
statement: Zone A is a tax lot located entirely in Manhattan south of 96th Street, or entirely in neighborhood tabulation areas BK0101 to BK0104 or QN0201. Zone B is a tax lot located entirely in BK0201 to BK0204, BK0601, BK0602, BK0801, QN0105 or QN0102. NTAs are as most recently defined by City Planning.
qualifiers: The labels do not mean Manhattan versus the outer boroughs.
The 485-x Zone A boundary at 96th Street is different from the zoning Manhattan Core.
questions: Is my site in 485-x Zone A?
What areas are 485-x Zone B?

title: 485-x construction and building service wages
statement: Construction wage floors apply per eligible site with 100 or more units. From July 1, 2026 the minimum is $42.03 per hour; for 150+ units in Zone A, the lesser of $76.12 or 65 percent of the greatest prevailing wage and supplements within a classification; for 150+ units in Zone B, the lesser of $66.19 or 60 percent. The statutory bases were $40.00, $72.45 and $63.00, rising 2.5 percent each July 1 from 2025. Rates cover wages and supplements combined, with up to 50 percent paid as supplements. Building service prevailing wages apply separately for the benefit period at 30 or more units, unless all units are affordable and at least 50 percent are at or below 90 percent AMI.
qualifiers: Project labor agreements and collective bargaining or jobsite agreements can exclude covered work only with an express waiver and notice to the Comptroller.
Missing the commencement notice risks fines up to $5,000 per day and loss of benefits.
HPD's page shows only the base rates; the Comptroller's table governs current rates.
misconceptions: Using the original $40 base instead of the current escalated rate.
questions: What is the 485-x wage requirement?
What is the 485-x wage rate in 2026?

title: How 485-x counts units: the eligible site
statement: 485-x unit thresholds are counted per eligible site: a tax lot containing an eligible multiple dwelling, or a zoning lot containing two or more eligible multiple dwellings that are part of a single application. The statute, HPD's rules and the Comptroller's rules contain no separate contiguity, common-ownership or anti-splitting rule. How HPD treats separately filed buildings on one zoning lot is unconfirmed.
qualifiers: Get counsel's view before relying on separate filings to stay under a threshold.
misconceptions: Describing a general statutory site-aggregation rule.
questions: Can I split a project to stay under 100 units for 485-x?
What is a 485-x eligible site?

title: Underwrite the 485-x unit thresholds
statement: Where the envelope allows, model 99, 100, 149 and 150 unit alternatives. At 100 units the construction wage floor starts and the benefit becomes a full 35 years; at 150 units in Zones A and B the affordability deepens to 60 percent AMI, wages rise and the benefit extends to 40 years. Compare residual land value across these cases rather than assuming the largest building wins.
qualifiers: Thresholds count units per eligible site; see the eligible-site fact before splitting buildings.
questions: Should I build 99 or 100 units?
How do 485-x thresholds affect project size?

title: ULURP review clocks
statement: After certification, the community board has 60 days, the borough president 30 days after the board's recommendation or deadline, and the City Planning Commission 60 days after the borough president's period. The City Council acts within 50 days of the Commission's filing with the Council, tolled up to 15 days when modifications are referred back to the Commission. The Mayor may disapprove within 5 days of receiving the Council's filing, and the Council can override by a two-thirds vote within 10 days. Pre-certification has no fixed time limit; after 6 months the applicant or borough president can in some cases appeal to the Commission.
qualifiers: Pre-certification and environmental review are usually the unpredictable parts of the schedule.
questions: How long does ULURP take?
What are the ULURP steps?

title: Map amendments, text amendments and Council review
statement: A map amendment changes the mapped district and generally follows ULURP; a text amendment changes the Zoning Resolution's rules and is adopted by the City Planning Commission by resolution after notice and a public hearing (Charter §200), not through ULURP. The Council automatically reviews zoning map and text changes, housing and urban renewal plans and residential dispositions. When the community board and borough president both recommend disapproval and the borough president objects within 5 days, Council review is required; the Council can call up other items by majority vote within 20 days.
qualifiers: An MIH text amendment filed with an ELURP application follows ELURP.
questions: What is the difference between a map and text amendment?
Does the City Council vote on every rezoning?

title: Expedited Land Use Review Procedure (ELURP)
statement: Charter amendments approved by voters on November 4, 2025 created ELURP (Charter §197-e). Eligible actions must use it instead of ULURP, including zoning map changes that increase maximum residential floor area by no more than 30 percent in R6 and higher areas, and low-density map changes with a standard height of 45 ft or less and FAR of 2.0. ELURP is a 90-day review: advisory review by the community board and borough president, then a final City Planning Commission decision with no City Council review. Outside Fast Track cases it is limited to actions that need no environmental impact statement. The Commission adopted implementing rules in 2026.
qualifiers: A large upzoning, such as R6A to R8A (roughly double the floor area), still goes through ULURP.
misconceptions: Treating every rezoning as a seven-month ULURP with a Council vote.
questions: What is ELURP?
Is there a faster review for small rezonings?
Does the Council vote on modest rezonings?

citations.label: CPC ELURP and AHAB rules, notice of adoption (2026)

title: Affordable Housing Fast Track
statement: The November 4, 2025 Charter amendments created an Affordable Housing Fast Track (Charter §197-f) that replaces ULURP for publicly funded affordable housing projects citywide and for projects creating affordable housing in the 12 community districts that have historically permitted the least affordable housing. Fast Track actions end at the City Planning Commission without a City Council vote.
qualifiers: Exact eligibility follows the Commission's Fast Track methodology rules; confirm the current district list and criteria before relying on it.
questions: What is the affordable housing fast track?
Which projects skip ULURP?

title: Affordable Housing Appeals Board
statement: The November 4, 2025 Charter amendments created an Affordable Housing Appeals Board (Charter §197-g) made up of the Mayor, the Council Speaker and the affected Borough President. On a request filed within 5 days of the Council's action, it may reverse within 15 days a Council disapproval or modification of a single-borough affordable housing application.
misconceptions: Assuming a Council disapproval of an affordable housing rezoning is always final.
questions: Can a Council rejection of affordable housing be overturned?
What is the Affordable Housing Appeals Board?

title: Pricing rezoning upside
statement: Pick the review track first: ELURP for modest upzonings (up to 30 percent more floor area in R6 and higher), Fast Track for qualifying affordable projects, ULURP for larger map changes. A rezoning needs a planning rationale, environmental documentation and public approvals; approval is uncertain and new districts are usually mapped with MIH, which changes the economics. Price theoretical floor area as an option, not as approved capacity, and use entitlement contingencies or adequate diligence when buying on rezoning upside.
misconceptions: Pricing theoretical rezoned FAR as if it were approved.
questions: How should I value rezoning potential?
Which approval path fits my rezoning?

title: Site feasibility worksheet
statement: For every site, get a coordinated attorney and architect package answering: surveyed zoning-lot area; district, overlays and every special district; standard FAR by use and mixed-use limits; qualifying FAR and whether UAP or MIH applies; existing floor area; legally available unused rights, title restrictions and prior transfers or declarations; achievable envelope including base heights, setbacks, the 20 ft or 30 ft rear yard, coverage and §23-443 height modifications; unit count from compliant floor plans and the dwelling unit factor; exclusions, transfers and bonuses; current parking and loading requirements; UAP, MIH and 485-x separately; landmarks, environmental conditions, infrastructure and flood risk; any rezoning action with its review track (ULURP, ELURP or Fast Track); entitlement timing, costs and risks; and residual land value for each scenario.
qualifiers: Also check existing tenancies, including rent-stabilized occupants and whether HPD's Certificate of No Harassment applies, since they can delay demolition; this item has not been verified against current rules.
questions: What should I check before buying a development site?
What goes into a zoning feasibility study?

title: Six numbers and three massing studies before buying
statement: Before buying, know: standard buildable zoning floor area; maximum realistically achievable zoning floor area; physical gross building area; net rentable or sellable area and achievable unit count; all-in development cost for each scenario; and residual land value after taxes, affordability and entitlement risk. Test three massing studies: standard as-of-right, maximum eligible as-of-right, and discretionary upside. The same lot area does not imply the same buildable form across districts.
qualifiers: Value framework: permitted floor area, lawfully available additional rights, permitted excluded area and architectural efficiency, weighed against the costs and burdens to achieve them.
questions: What numbers do I need before buying a site?
Which massing scenarios should I test?

title: Development site acquisition strategies
statement: As-of-right optimization: look for unused FAR, assemblage potential, eligible affordable density and inefficient existing buildings, preferring sites where a substantially larger building is already permitted; entitlement risk is lower but feasibility and permit risk remain. Air rights and assemblage: find underbuilt neighbors next to strong sites and secure rights only after confirming a valid merger or transfer and an efficient envelope. Rezoning and conversions: study appropriately located industrial or commercial sites, underused transit-adjacent parcels and eligible conversion buildings, separating ELURP-scale or Fast Track rezonings from ULURP-scale ones because their timing and risk differ.
questions: How do developers find sites with upside?
What are the main development strategies in NYC?

title: Four questions for any site's capacity
statement: Ask in order: how much floor area is legally permitted; how much physically fits within the envelope; what additional capacity is lawfully available through affordability, transfers, mergers, bonuses or exclusions; and which scenario produces the highest residual value. Extra FAR alone does not create extra height, and heights are stated in feet, not stories.
misconceptions: Converting height limits into a fixed story count.
questions: How do I estimate what can be built on a lot?
